conclusion: Every soundcalc parameter that could be re-derived from a vendor's own source re-derived exactly, 51 of 51 numeric fields across RISC0, Miden, OpenVM and SP1, and soundcalc at its pin reproduces its own reports byte-for-byte. The failures are all in provenance rather than in arithmetic: two of eight cited pins do not resolve, a third names a tag that does not contain the generator credited with producing it, two units' reports cannot be regenerated by the code at HEAD at all, and four units ship no reproduction path.
confidence: Lean hard on the reproduction numbers and on the pin resolutions: both are mechanical, both are re-runnable by `probe.py`, and six planted faults each turned the verdict they should. Lean less on the interventions-per-unit figure of 1.5, which is a judgment count no code produces, and treat the SP1 verdict as scoped rather than complete: 30 of its 42 numeric fields were derived from source constants and the other 12 come from `machine.shape()` at runtime, which needs the Rust build this run did not do. FRESHNESS `unchanged` for RISC0 means only that the cited September 2024 notebook is byte-identical today, not that the vendor's prover is unchanged, and the write-up says so at the point of use.

core_candidates.what: Re-derive a config generator's output from its source constants instead of building and running it: read the constants the generator imports at a pinned ref, reimplement its arithmetic, and compare field by field, naming the fields that genuinely need runtime and refusing to guess them
core_candidates.why_reusable: It turned a ten-runner-hour Rust build budget into zero build minutes and still produced 30 of SP1's 42 fields, at two separate vendor refs. Any vendor that ships a generator computing mostly named-constant arithmetic is reproducible this way, and the technique also survives a compute-discipline rule that forbids the build outright. Its honest limit is built in: the fields needing runtime are enumerated rather than approximated.
core_candidates.first_step: Fulcrum decides whether a third non-mathematical instance is worth funding. If so, try this route first on any unit before costing a build, and measure how often it covers a useful fraction of the fields.

core_candidates.what: Ask the git server whether a cited commit exists, rather than asking a hosting API: `git fetch --depth 1 <url> <sha>` makes the server resolve the object and answer `not our ref`
core_candidates.why_reusable: It is one line, it is host-independent, and it is the check that produced this hunt's Airbender finding. A provenance audit that trusts an API for existence is trusting one vendor's index; the git protocol answers from the object store.
core_candidates.first_step: None needed to reuse it; it is five lines in `probe.py:ref_exists`. Worth folding into any future provenance probe rather than abstracting into a module.

core_candidates.what: A recurring pin-decay measurement: re-run the pin-resolution stage of a published accounting on a schedule and record how many of its cited sources have stopped resolving
core_candidates.why_reusable: Provenance rot is a rate, and nobody appears to measure it. This hunt produced one data point (2 of 8 dead in about six months) and cannot turn it into a rate alone. The instrument already exists as `probe.py pins` and costs seconds.
core_candidates.first_step: Fulcrum decides whether a standing monthly run is worth a slot. Do not build scheduling machinery here; `harness/VERDICT.md` is the reason.

notes_for_operator: No unit is held. No unit produced a REPRODUCTION mismatch at all, so the disclosure hold never engaged, and everything found is published in full. The one judgment call worth your eye is Venus: its TOML header claims parameters identical to ZisK's and one circuit of forty-four differs in seven numeric fields. I published it, with the reasoning stated in RESULTS.md so you can overrule me: every per-regime total is identical between the two reports, each system's headline is 128 bits either way, and the differing component is ALI, which is not the binding term. If you read that differently, the section to pull is 'Venus: the header's equivalence claim does not hold'. Two corrections to the brief, both confirmed by your mid-run messages and handled as you said: CLOSE THE LOOP's premise is wrong, this came from issue #140 and not from a harness function, so no ledger entry was manufactured and the genuinely open ledger items are named in RESULTS.md instead; and the required_checks about the zeta package do not apply, though for the record the venv does install and `import zeta` does work here, this hunt simply uses nothing from it and probe.py is stdlib-only plus a pinned `toml` in its own venv. Hunt number #109 was free. One allocation question, yours not mine: about one runner-hour of Rust build on CI would close SP1's remaining twelve fields, and it is the only place in this hunt where money buys a strictly better verdict.
